ch54.anchor: the quarter of the demon gate
ch54.note: The kimon or “demon gate” is the northeast, the unlucky quarter in Chinese and Japanese geomancy, from which evil influences and misfortune were held to come; a house or a castle was sited with an eye to warding it. Kondō, a farmer’s son with no learning in such things, is uneasy all the same to find his camp lying to the northeast of Edo.

Mirin is a sweet, low-alcohol rice liquor used in cooking; Nagareyama was, and remains, a noted center of its brewing. The great warehouses of sweet mash are Shiba’s explanation for the town’s plague of mosquitoes.

ch54.anchor: A billet-board hung at the entrance
ch54.note: A sekifuda was a wooden placard hung at the gate of a lodging to announce the name and rank of the traveler putting up there, in the manner of an official on progress. By hanging one that read “Ōkubo Yamato,” Toshizō dresses the muster up as the lawful billet of a shogunal officer rather than a rebel camp.

A tsubo is the standard Japanese unit of floor and land area, about 3.3 square meters, the size of two tatami mats laid together. Three thousand tsubo is close to a hectare, or roughly two and a half acres.

ch54.anchor: having already pacified the post-towns of the Tōkaidō
ch54.note: The daisōtokufu, the field headquarters of the new government’s eastern expedition, was nominally under Prince Arisugawa Taruhito as Grand Marshal. Advancing along the Tōkaidō, the coast road up from Kyoto, it had reached Sunpu (modern Shizuoka) by the third month of 1868 and made it the staging point for the march on Edo.

ch54.anchor: reached Itabashi on the thirteenth of the third month
ch54.note: Itabashi was the first post-station on the Nakasendō, the inland highway, just northwest of Edo. Here the new government’s Tōsandō vanguard fixed its main camp; the station also held one of Edo’s execution grounds, a circumstance that will matter to Kondō before the month is out.

Historically Kondō gave himself up on Keiō 4/4/3 (25 April 1868), still passing as the shogunal officer “Ōkubo Yamato,” in the hope of sparing his farmer-levy. He was carried off to the new government’s camp, his true identity was established there, and he was put to death soon after; the manner of it is told in a later chapter.

A bukan was a printed directory of the daimyō and of the shogunate’s own officials, listing each man’s name, crest, stipend, and post. That the name “Ōkubo Yamato” stood in no bukan told Itagaki at once that it was an alias, and that its bearer was traveling under a false shogunal rank.

Sakamoto Ryōma and Nakaoka Shintarō were cut down at the Ōmiya lodging-house in Kyoto in the eleventh month of 1867. The killing is now generally laid to the Kyoto Mimawarigumi under Sasaki Tadasaburō; the Tosa men’s conviction that it was the Shinsengumi’s work, voiced here, was widely held at the time but is not borne out by the later evidence. It fed their hatred of the corps all the same.

ch54.anchor: a man of grave and imposing bearing appeared
ch54.note: The scene that follows is drawn from Satō Gennosuke’s own later account of his interrogation. As with the Hino homecoming of an earlier chapter, Shiba quotes a surviving family recollection directly rather than inventing the exchange.

ch54.anchor: the Rikuentai, the rōnin corps of the Tosa domain
ch54.note: The Rikuentai (“Land Auxiliary Force”) and the Kaientai (“Naval Auxiliary Force”) were the two private companies of Tosa masterless men led, respectively, by Nakaoka Shintarō and Sakamoto Ryōma: the one drilled as a land militia, the other traded and ran ships in the loyalist cause. Both lost their captains in the Ōmiya killing.

ch54.anchor: the great cause and the rightful name
ch54.note: Taigi-meibun is the Confucian principle that binds a man to his rightful lord and to the legitimate order of things, and brands a stand against them as rebellion. Kondō, who has spent the war insisting the Tokugawa cause was the lawful one, now reads the Emperor’s banner as having carried that legitimacy away with it; to fight on would be to die a rebel. It is on this, and not on courage, that he and Toshizō at last divide.

Ōshū is the old name for Mutsu, the great province of the far northeast. Here it stands for the northern domains — Aizu chief among them — still under arms against the new government, and so for the war Toshizō means to go on fighting.
